scenes.title: Share input tiles without changing the result.
Larger tiles also consume block resources.
Write a hypothesis and its uncertainty.
Different counts grow at different rates.
Turn the model into a testable recommendation.

cues.text: Chapter Fourteen investigates one matrix multiplication. Keep the inputs, dimensions, number format and final output fixed while changing how input values are reused.
The baseline computes sixteen outputs separately. Its teaching algorithm explicitly loads one hundred and twenty-eight input values and stores sixteen results.
A tile width of two shares loaded inputs across several outputs and reduces the count to sixty-four input loads. A width of four reduces it to thirty-two.
Every choice produces the same complete output matrix in this model. These are explicit algorithm loads with cache reuse excluded; they are not measured physical memory traffic.
With the chapter’s synthetic resource budgets, tile width two uses thirty-two shared-memory bytes and two hundred and fifty-six registers per block. Four blocks fit those budgets.

Tile width four uses one hundred and twenty-eight shared-memory bytes and one thousand and twenty-four registers per block. Only one block fits. This capacity bound is not a schedule or a timing measurement.
A useful recommendation states both the benefit and the cost. A larger tile reduces explicit input loads while using more registers and shared memory per block.
Either tile can be a hypothesis worth investigating. Neither a lower load count nor a higher block capacity proves which implementation is faster on a physical GPU.
Now use eight-by-eight inputs with tile width two and the same resource budgets. Predict input loads, output stores and resident-block capacity.
Does doubling the matrix dimension double every count? Separate complete-operation counts from resources needed by one block before comparing the answer.
This eight-by-eight case loads five hundred and twelve input values and stores sixty-four outputs. Four blocks still fit the stated teaching budgets.
At fixed tile width, input loads grow with the cube of the matrix dimension, while output stores grow with its square. The resources used by one block do not change here.
To compare real implementations, first check both outputs against a suitable reference. Keep inputs and number format comparable, and change one proposed optimisation at a time.
Define whether timing includes allocation and transfers. Warm up, wait for the GPU work in the chosen interval, repeat measurements, and inspect actual operations with a profiler.
The browser supports a reuse argument and a resource trade-off. It does not identify the fastest kernel or measure physical GPU performance.
Return to Chapter Fourteen and write your recommendation: which tile would you test first, what evidence supports it, what uncertainty remains, and what measurement would resolve it?
